title: Ways Up the Staircase
statement:
A staircase has n steps. You start at the bottom (step 0), and each move climbs either 1 step or 2 steps.

Return how many different sequences of moves end exactly on step n. Order matters: 1 then 2 and 2 then 1 are two different sequences.

examples.why: 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 1+2+1, 2+1+1 and 2+2. Counting only which step sizes are used (ignoring order) would give 3, which is wrong.
A single 1-step move. A 2-step move would overshoot, and overshooting does not count.
The last move lands on step 6 from step 5 (8 ways to get there) or from step 4 (5 ways). 8 + 5 = 13.

hints: Do not try to list sequences. Think about the very last move of any sequence that ends on step n. What can it be?
The last move is a 1-step from step n − 1 or a 2-step from step n − 2. Every way to reach step n is a way to reach one of those two, plus that last move.

Let ways(i) be the number of sequences that end on step i. Then ways(i) = ways(i − 1) + ways(i − 2), with ways(0) = 1 and ways(1) = 1. Fill it from small i to large i; you only ever need the last two values.

explain.intuition:
This problem is the cleanest place to learn the dynamic programming routine. Every DP problem in this section is solved with the same five moves, so it is worth doing them slowly once.

1. State, in words. ways(i) = the number of move sequences that start at step 0 and end exactly on step i. The answer is ways(n). 2. Recurrence. Split all sequences that end on i by their last move. If it was a 1-step, what came before is any sequence ending on i − 1; if it was a 2-step, any sequence ending on i − 2. The two groups do not overlap and together cover everything, so ways(i) = ways(i − 1) + ways(i − 2). 3. Base cases. ways(0) = 1 (the empty sequence: you are already there) and ways(1) = 1. 4. Order of filling. Each value needs the two smaller ones, so fill i = 2, 3, …, n. 5. Implementation, three ways. Plain recursion recomputes the same ways(i) again and again, so it grows like 1.6ⁿ. Add a memo (a cache keyed by i, like memoising a selector) and every state is computed once: O(n). Turn it into a table filled left to right and the recursion disappears. Then notice the table only ever reads its last two cells, so two variables are enough: O(1) space.
steps: State: ways(i) = number of move sequences from step 0 that end exactly on step i.
Recurrence: ways(i) = ways(i − 1) + ways(i − 2), split by whether the last move was 1 or 2 steps.
Order: i from 2 up to n, so both smaller values exist when you need them.
Space: the table reads only ways(i − 1) and ways(i − 2), so keep two variables prev2, prev1 and slide them forward.
pitfalls: Setting ways(0) = 0. Then ways(2) = ways(1) + ways(0) = 1, but 1+1 and 2 are two ways. Standing still at the bottom is one (empty) way to be on step 0.
Plain recursion without a cache. It is correct, but n = 45 takes over a billion calls because ways(43) is recomputed from both ways(45) and ways(44), and so on down.
Counting combinations instead of sequences. For n = 4 there are 3 multisets of step sizes but 5 orderings.

solutions.title: Plain recursion
solutions.idea: Write the recurrence directly. Correct, but the same sub-answers are recomputed an exponential number of times.

solutions.title: Recursion with a memo
solutions.idea: Same recursion, but cache each ways(i) the first time it is computed. Each of the n + 1 states is solved once.

solutions.title: Table, filled bottom-up
solutions.idea: Store ways(i) in an array and fill it from the base cases upward. No recursion at all.

solutions.title: Two rolling variables
solutions.idea: The table only ever reads its last two cells, so keep just those two and slide them forward.

followups: Each move can climb 1, 2 or 3 steps. What changes in the recurrence and the base cases?
The allowed step sizes come in a list, and some steps are broken and cannot be stood on. Generalise the solution.
n can be up to 10¹⁸ and the answer is wanted modulo 10⁹ + 7. How do you avoid a loop of length n? (Hint: a 2 × 2 matrix.)
